title: Islands that get older in a line
teaches: How a nearly fixed source of magma under a moving plate builds a chain of volcanoes, and what the Hawaiian-Emperor bend records

parts.title: Volcanoes in the middle of a plate

blocks.text: Hawaii does not fit the pattern of lesson 10. The islands stand in the middle of the Pacific plate, more than 3,000 kilometres from the nearest plate boundary, yet Kīlauea and Mauna Loa are among the most active volcanoes on Earth. The chain they belong to has a peculiar arrangement: the islands get steadily older, and more worn down, toward the northwest.

blocks.caption: The main Hawaiian islands, with the approximate ages of their volcanoes. Only the island of Hawaiʻi, at the southeast end, has continuously active volcanoes.

options.title: The Hawaiian Islands
options.alt: A shaded relief map of the main Hawaiian Islands and the surrounding sea floor, from Kauaʻi in the northwest to the island of Hawaiʻi in the southeast.

blocks.text: The difference is visible from the air. On the island of Hawaiʻi, fresh lava flows are bare black rock, and the volcanoes are broad, smooth domes. Maui is greener and gullied. Oʻahu's volcanoes have been carved into sharp ridges and deep valleys, and Kauaʻi, the oldest of the main islands, is cut by canyons nearly a kilometre deep. The American geologist James Dwight Dana noted this progression in 1840 while sailing with the United States Exploring Expedition. Hawaiian oral tradition had arrived at a similar order long before: the volcano goddess Pele moved from island to island, from Kauaʻi toward the southeast, digging crater pits that flooded with sea water until she finally settled at Kīlauea.

blocks.caption: The Hawaiian islands from the International Space Station. The island of Hawaiʻi, the largest and youngest, is at the lower right.

blocks.text: Radioactive dating of the lavas (lesson 7) later put numbers on the sequence. The main shield volcano of Kauaʻi formed about 5 million years ago, those of Oʻahu between 2.6 and 3.7 million, those of Molokaʻi about 1.8 million, and the two shields of Maui between 1.3 and 0.8 million. Beyond Kauaʻi the chain continues northwest as tiny rocky islands, coral atolls, and drowned underwater volcanoes known as **seamounts**, growing older all the way: Midway, 2,400 kilometres from Kīlauea, is about 28 million years old.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Hawaii's volcanoes lie in the middle of the Pacific plate, more than 3,000 km from any plate boundary.
The volcanoes get progressively older and more eroded toward the northwest, from active Kīlauea to 5-million-year-old Kauaʻi and 28-million-year-old Midway.

parts.title: A plate passing over a hotspot

blocks.text: In 1963 the Canadian geophysicist J. Tuzo Wilson suggested a physical mechanism. Suppose a source of magma deep in the mantle stays in one place while the oceanic plate slides over it. A volcano grows directly above the source, gets carried away by the moving plate, loses its supply of magma, and goes extinct, while a new volcano begins to build over the source behind it. The result is a line of volcanoes getting steadily older in the direction of plate motion, much like the scorch trail left on a sheet of paper pulled slowly across a candle flame.

That stationary magma source came to be known as a **hotspot**. In 1971 W. Jason Morgan proposed that hotspots are fed by **mantle plumes**, narrow columns of unusually hot solid rock rising slowly from deep in the mantle, perhaps from as far down as the boundary with the outer core. As this hot rock nears the surface, the weight of overlying rock decreases, and the drop in pressure allows it to partly melt without needing the water that triggers melting above subduction zones. Today the Hawaiian plume sits beneath the island of Hawaiʻi, and the next volcano in the chain, Kamaʻehuakanaloa (formerly Lōʻihi), is already growing on the sea floor about 35 kilometres off the island's southeast coast, its summit still a kilometre below the waves.
If the hotspot stays put, the ages of the volcanoes record the speed of the plate: distance from the hotspot divided by age.

blocks.caption: The Hawaiian-Emperor chain as seen from above, with the plume fixed under Kīlauea. Circles are dated volcanoes; red dots are where volcanoes would be if the plate moved at the chosen speed, with its change of direction 47 million years ago (volcanoes older than that lie to the north). Below: age against distance from Kīlauea.
blocks.task: Set the plate's speed so the model's volcanoes fall on the dated ones

blocks.text: A rate of about 8 to 10 centimetres a year puts the model dots on the dated islands. That is among the fastest plate speeds on Earth, and it matches the rate at which the Pacific plate moves relative to neighbouring plates, worked out independently from magnetic stripes on the sea floor.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A hotspot is a long-lived magma source beneath a moving plate, fed by decompression melting in a rising mantle plume.
As the plate carries each volcano away from the magma supply, the volcano goes extinct and a new one forms behind it.
Dividing a volcano's distance from Kīlauea by its age gives the Pacific plate's speed: about 8 to 10 cm a year.

blocks.text: Northwest of Midway, the line of drowned volcanoes continues for another 1,100 kilometres and then bends sharply to the north. This northern arm, the **Emperor Seamounts**, runs toward the Aleutian Islands and ends near the Kamchatka Peninsula, where the oldest seamounts in the chain, around 80 million years old, arrive at the trench and are subducted. The volcanoes right at the bend are about 47 million years old.

For decades the bend was read purely as a sudden swerve by the Pacific plate about 47 million years ago: before then it moved roughly north, building the Emperor chain, and afterward it moved west-northwest, building the Hawaiian chain. Then in 2001 an ocean drilling expedition cored lavas from several Emperor Seamounts and measured their ancient magnetism. Because the Earth's magnetic field lines run horizontal at the magnetic equator and dip more steeply into the ground closer to the poles, the dip angle frozen into a cooling lava records the latitude where it erupted. The Emperor lavas turned out to have formed well north of Hawaii's present latitude at 19° N; Detroit Seamount, near the northern end, erupted at about 36° N. Between 80 and 47 million years ago, the plume itself was drifting south through the convecting mantle, and the sharp bend reflects both a change in Pacific plate motion and the slowing or halting of the plume's southward drift.
Hotspots, then, are not anchored in place. Even so, they wander much more slowly than the plates overhead, so a hotspot track remains a reliable trace of where a plate has travelled.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: About 3,500 km northwest of Kīlauea, at volcanoes 47 million years old, the chain bends north to become the Emperor Seamounts.

Magnetic inclinations in Emperor Seamount lavas show that the plume drifted south from about 36° N to 19° N before 47 million years ago, so the bend reflects both plume drift and a change in plate motion.

blocks.text: A Hawaiian volcano follows a predictable arc from birth to submergence. Measured from the surrounding sea floor, Mauna Kea and Mauna Loa stand more than 9 kilometres tall, higher from base to peak than Mount Everest. That immense load flexes the underlying oceanic plate downward, so the island is already subsiding while its lavas are still piling up. Once the plate carries the volcano off the hotspot, it sinks further for two reasons: it rides down the flank of the broad, buoyant swell of warm mantle rock around the plume, and the oceanic plate beneath it continues to cool, thicken, and settle lower into the mantle as it ages.

blocks.caption: Pahoehoe lava at Kīlauea, its skin wrinkling into ropes as it cools, with molten rock glowing beneath. Flow upon flow like this builds a shield volcano.

blocks.text: At the same time, rain and ocean waves attack the exposed rock. In warm tropical waters, coral reefs build up around the island's shores. As the volcanic peak subsides, living coral grows upward to stay in the sunlit surface water, until the last volcanic rock slips below the waves and only a ring of coral reef remains around a shallow lagoon: an **atoll**, such as Midway. Charles Darwin worked out this exact sequence for coral atolls in 1842, more than a century before geologists understood why volcanic islands sink in the first place. Farther northwest, the plate carries the atolls into cooler waters where coral growth cannot keep pace with subsidence, and the islands drown completely. Many become flat-topped seamounts known as **guyots**, whose summits were planed flat by wave erosion when they stood at sea level.

blocks.caption: Midway Atoll, a ring of coral reef around a shallow lagoon. The volcano that built it has sunk out of sight.

blocks.text: Hotspot tracks also cross continents. In the American West, the Snake River Plain slices across southern Idaho as a depression of volcanic calderas that get systematically younger toward the northeast, culminating in the active geothermal system at Yellowstone. Here the North American plate is sliding southwest over a mantle plume; the oldest calderas along the track, near the junction of Idaho, Oregon, and Nevada, erupted about 16 to 17 million years ago, around the same time the flood lavas of the Columbia River basalts poured out across eastern Washington and Oregon.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Volcanic islands subside under their own weight, by riding off the warm swell above the plume, and as the underlying plate cools and contracts.
Upward-growing coral reefs on a subsiding volcano form a ring-shaped atoll; once carried into colder water, the volcano drowns completely to become a seamount or flat-topped guyot.
The Snake River Plain and Yellowstone mark a continental hotspot track built as the North American plate moves southwest over a plume.

blocks.caption: Five questions on hotspots
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why do the Hawaiian islands get progressively older toward the northwest?
choices: The Pacific plate moves northwest over a deep magma source, carrying each volcano away from its supply
Magma takes longer to rise through the thicker crust in the southeast
A plate boundary is unzipping slowly from northwest to southeast
items.why: As the plate slides northwest over the plume, each volcano is carried off the magma source and goes extinct while a new one forms behind it.

items.ask: A volcano 1,060 km northwest of Kīlauea is 10.3 million years old. Roughly how fast has the Pacific plate moved over that span?
items.why: 1,060 km divided by 10.3 million years is about 103 km per million years, which equals 103 mm or roughly 10 cm a year.

items.ask: What causes mantle rock to melt beneath a hotspot?
choices: Hot rock rises in a plume and partly melts as the pressure on it drops near the surface
Water released from a subducting slab lowers the mantle's melting point
Friction between the moving plate and the stationary mantle heats the base of the crust
items.why: Plume rock is already unusually hot; as it rises toward the surface, the falling pressure allows it to partly melt without needing water.

items.ask: What did the magnetic dip angles frozen into lavas from the Emperor Seamounts reveal?
choices: The lavas erupted much farther north than Hawaii's present latitude, showing that the plume itself had drifted south
The lavas erupted at Hawaii's present latitude of 19° N, proving the plume never moved
The Emperor chain was built by a separate northern hotspot unrelated to Hawaii
items.why: Magnetic inclination records the latitude of cooling; Detroit Seamount formed near 36° N compared with 19° N for Hawaii today, showing that the plume drifted south before 47 million years ago.

items.ask: How did Charles Darwin explain the formation of a coral atoll like Midway?
choices: A fringing reef keeps growing upward to stay in sunlit water while the volcanic island beneath it slowly sinks
Corals colonize the rim of a submerged volcanic crater that never reached the surface
Storm waves pile broken coral sand into a circular bar on a flat sea floor
items.why: Darwin deduced in 1842 that fringing reefs turn into barrier reefs and then ring-shaped atolls as the central volcanic peak subsides below sea level.

learned: Hawaii sits above a hotspot, a long-lived magma source fed by decompression melting in a rising mantle plume, far from any plate boundary.
As the Pacific plate slides northwest over the hotspot, it carries volcanoes away from their magma supply; dividing distance by age gives a plate speed of 8 to 10 cm a year.
The 47-million-year-old bend between the Hawaiian and Emperor chains records both a change in Pacific plate motion and the end of the plume's southward drift.
Volcanic islands sink under their own weight and as the plate cools, evolving into coral atolls and then drowned seamounts and flat-topped guyots.
